title: why meditation starts and ends with a sound
hook: why meditation starts and ends with a sound

segments.voice: Yesterday: sati, remembering to notice, the gatekeeper at the gate. Your line was notice. What ordinary thing did you do start to finish? Day ten.

Every one of these lessons has started with a sound. You've heard it ten times now. Maybe you've stopped hearing it. In meditation halls around the world, from a monastery in Thailand to a Zen temple in Kyoto to a church basement where a group sits on Tuesday nights, something similar happens. Someone strikes a bell. Everyone goes quiet. Minutes later, the bell again, and people stretch and blink. Why a bell? Why not a timer, or someone saying okay, start? Today, the sound you've been hearing since day one.
screen: `TEN DAYS, THE SAME SOUND.` → `A BELL, AND EVERYONE GOES QUIET.` → `WHY A BELL?`

segments.voice: Bells go back a long way in Buddhist life. Temples in China, Korea and Japan hang great bronze bells struck with a swinging wooden beam, and across Buddhist Asia, bells, bowls, gongs and wooden boards mark the monastic day: time to wake, time to eat, time to sit. In Japan, on New Year's Eve, temples ring their great bell a hundred and eight times; tradition says one strike for each of the heart's hundred and eight troubles. At some temples, people line up in the cold to take a turn. But the plainest reason for a bell is right here in these lessons. A bell is a sound that begins, and then fades, and then is gone. You can follow it all the way down to silence. And following it is a tiny meditation all by itself, because the mind has to arrive in the present to hear it at all. The Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught his communities to stop whatever they're doing when a bell sounds, even mid-sentence, and take three breaths. He asked people not to say they hit the bell, but that they invite it to sound. A small change of words: the bell isn't a starting gun. It's a welcome. There's another thing a bell does. It holds the time for you. When the bell will tell you when to stop, you don't need to peek at the clock. You're free to just be here. That's why this app ends every sit with it. The bell keeps the time so you don't have to.
screen: `BELLS MARK THE MONASTIC DAY.` · `A HUNDRED AND EIGHT STRIKES.` · `A SOUND YOU FOLLOW TO SILENCE.` · `INVITE THE BELL, DON'T HIT IT.` · then, large: `THE BELL HOLDS THE TIME.`

segments.voice: When the bell sounds this time, don't just wait for it to be over. Follow it. Listen to the strike, then the ring, then the long fade, all the way down until you can't tell if you're still hearing it. Then stay there, in whatever's left, for the rest of the forty-five seconds. When your mind wanders, you'll hear the next bell to call you back. The bell holds the time.
The bell. A sound that begins and fades, calling the mind into the present, and holding the time so you don't have to. Tenth word.
Your line: arrive. Choose a sound you'll hear today, a phone buzz, a door, a kettle, and let it be your bell: when it sounds, stop and take one breath. Day ten.

howItsDone: In many Buddhist temples and meditation groups, a bell or gong opens and closes each sitting and marks the monastic day; in Plum Village communities people pause and breathe whenever a bell sounds, and in Japan temples ring their great bell 108 times on New Year's Eve.

options: ignore it. it's for the monks.
fork.reveal: they stop, even mid-sentence, and take a few breaths. the bell is a call back to the present, for everyone.

what a scholar hears: bells, gongs and wooden boards order the monastic day across Asia; joya no kane, the 108 New Year's Eve strikes, count the 108 kleshas, the heart's afflictions, in Japanese tradition.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: the great beam-struck bronze bell is East Asian, so 'temples across Asia' became China, Korea and Japan; the 108 count is now 'tradition says'; cut 'you can't listen to a bell yesterday' (echoes day 2's 'you can't breathe yesterday's breath') and the stock 'it tells you everything'.
The 108 strikes and the 108 afflictions (bonno): confirm the count and the explanation, which varies by source.
Thich Nhat Hanh named and paraphrased (never quoted): 'invite the bell', stop and breathe when it sounds. Confirm the paraphrase; Plum Village practice is usually three breaths.
No original-language word given (the bell has many names across Buddhist languages); original set to null.
